summary: This RFC describes layering CMP over HTTP and includes the RFC 9480 updates introducing CMP URIs with a well-known prefix. It obsoletes RFC 6712 and, together with RFC 9810, obsoletes RFC 9480.

plainLanguage.summary: The certificate forms need a delivery truck. This explains how to send them across the ordinary web.

subtitle: How to carry Certificate Management Protocol messages over plain HTTP POST requests, with a well-known URL prefix.

tldr.problem: The Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) needs a transfer mechanism so end entities, registration authorities and certification authorities can pass PKIMessage structures to each other, with connection and error handling.
tldr.mechanism: Each DER-encoded PKIMessage is sent as the content of an HTTP POST request with media type application/pkixcmp, and the reply comes back in the HTTP response. Servers support the path prefix /.well-known/cmp.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 6712 and, together with RFC 9810, RFC 9480. It folds in the well-known URI changes from RFC 9480 and drops the HTTP/1.0 requirement.

facts.label: Success status for a CMP response

today: RFC 9811 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2025. It obsoletes RFC 6712 and, together with RFC 9810, RFC 9480, and no later RFC is listed as replacing or updating it.

sections.title: Why CMP Rides on HTTP
sections.content:
The Certificate Management Protocol (CMP, RFC 9810) needs a well-defined way for End Entities (EEs), Registration Authorities (RAs) and Certification Authorities (CAs) to pass PKIMessage structures between them. The remaining features CMP wants from a transfer protocol are connection and error handling, and HTTP covers both.

The RFC admits that using only the POST method effectively tunnels CMP over HTTP, which is generally considered bad practice. It gives its reasons: HTTP is easy to implement, it can cross network borders through ubiquitous proxies, and it is already commonly used in existing CMP implementations. GET and other methods are not used because PKI management operations can only be triggered by CMP's PKI messages, which need a POST.

HTTP is stateless, but that is not a blocker. CMP carries its own transactionID, so a transaction that spans more than one request and response pair can still be followed.
sections.plainLanguage: The web already knows how to carry messages and report when something goes wrong. So instead of building a new delivery system, CMP just uses it.

sections.title: Requests, Responses and the Media Type
sections.content:
A DER-encoded PKIMessage MUST be sent as the content of an HTTP POST request. If the request succeeds, the server returns the CMP response in the content of the HTTP response, and the status code MUST be 200 (OK). Other 2xx codes MUST NOT be used for this purpose.

The Internet media type application/pkixcmp MUST be set in the Content-Type header field when conveying a PKIMessage.

Error statuses are allowed too. All applicable 4xx and 5xx codes MAY be used to inform the client about errors. Whenever a client receives a response with a status code in the 2xx, 4xx or 5xx ranges, it MUST support handling response content that holds a CMP response PKIMessage.
sections.plainLanguage: You put your filled-in form in the envelope and mark it with the right label. If everything goes well, the answer comes back with a plain 200 stamp. Even when something goes wrong, the reply may still hold a proper answer.

sections.title: Communication Workflow and Redirects
sections.content:
In CMP, most communication starts at the EE, and every CMP request triggers a CMP response from the CA or RA. Some operations need several request and response pairs; the transaction identifier in the CMP message header ties them together.

If the receipt of an HTTP request is not confirmed by an HTTP response, it MUST be assumed that the CMP message was not delivered.

Redirection 3xx status codes MAY be supported, but clients should only follow them automatically after careful thought about the security implications. The RFC notes that a 301 (Moved Permanently) response could be misused for permanent denial of service.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask, they answer. If no answer comes back, assume your letter never arrived. And do not blindly follow a note that says the office has moved, since it could be a trick.

sections.title: Well-Known CMP URIs
sections.content:
Each CMP server on a PKI management entity that supports HTTP or HTTPS MUST support the path prefix /.well-known/ with the registered name cmp. This eases interworking in a multi-vendor setup.

Clients need to be configured with enough information to form the server URI: at least the authority portion, such as www.example.com:80, or the full operation path. Further path segments MAY follow the registered name. The segment p followed by an arbitrary label could, for example, tell apart specific CAs or certificate profiles, and an operation label could name a PKI management operation (as in the Lightweight CMP Profile, RFC 9483).

  • http://www.example.com/.well-known/cmp
  • http://www.example.com/.well-known/cmp/<operation>
  • http://www.example.com/.well-known/cmp/p/<name>
  • http://www.example.com/.well-known/cmp/p/<name>/<operation>

https can be used instead of http.
sections.plainLanguage: Every CMP server keeps its front door at the same agreed spot, so any client knows where to knock. Extra signs on the door can point to a particular office or task.

sections.title: Pushing Announcements
sections.content:
A CMP server may create announcements when events occur or on a regular basis. It MAY use HTTP to push them to a suitable recipient, such as a repository or directory service. Here the CMP server acts as the HTTP client. The announcement types are CA Key Update Announcement, Certificate Announcement, Revocation Announcement and CRL Announcement. PKIMessage structures MUST be sent as the content of an HTTP POST request.

No CMP response is needed, but the recipient MUST acknowledge receipt with an HTTP response that has an appropriate status code and empty content. If none arrives, delivery must be assumed to have failed, and the sender MAY retry after a suitable wait.

  • 201 (Created): the announced item was stored or already present. This MUST be the answer in that case.
  • 202 (Accepted): the item was only accepted for further processing, so the sender may try again later.
  • A suitable 4xx or 5xx code MUST be returned when a problem occurs.

An EE that wants to poll for a CA key update or the current CRL can use a PKI Information Request instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the office sends out a notice on its own. The receiver does not write back a letter; it only sends a short receipt saying it got the notice.

sections.title: What Changed From RFC 6712 and RFC 9480
sections.content:
RFC 9480 updated RFC 6712 to support the Lightweight CMP Profile. It introduced the URI path prefix /.well-known/cmp, added ways to extend the URI with further segments, and defined a new protocol registry group for them. This document includes those changes.

It adds three more changes:

  • The requirement to support HTTP/1.0 is removed, in line with RFC 9205.
  • Implementations MUST forward CMP messages when an HTTP error status code occurs.
  • Section 3.8 of RFC 6712 is removed because it duplicates the current HTTP specifications.

The implementation notes add that other implementations may transfer CMP over HTTP differently. Implementations based on earlier documents might use an unregistered application/pkixcmp-poll media type, which conforming implementations MAY handle like application/pkixcmp.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the updated rulebook. It keeps the newer rules about where the front door is, drops an old requirement nobody needs, and tidies up the parts that repeated other rulebooks.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All security considerations of HTTP (RFC 9110) apply. The RFC adds five items for implementers and users.

  • Many open connections can exhaust resources, so idle connections should be closed after a suitable timeout.
  • Without TLS or HTTP digests there is no integrity protection at the HTTP level. Information from HTTP should not be used to change the state of the transaction, even when TLS or digests are used.
  • Storing the target of a 301 response could let an attacker in the middle block a client from reaching the right server.
  • Unless HTTP responses to pushed announcements are authenticated and protected, their processing information may not be trusted, so the PKI design must not depend on announcements being reliably received.
  • CMP has its own integrity protection and authentication, and unencrypted CMP content is not sensitive enough to endanger the PKI. An eavesdropper might still learn personal, technical or business information, so users should consider HTTP over TLS or a virtual private network such as IPsec.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not leave doors open forever, do not trust a note that was not sealed, and use a locked tunnel if you want nobody to peek at who is asking for what.

sections.title: IANA Updates
sections.content:
IANA has updated four registry entries so they point to this document. No further IANA action is needed.

  • The application/pkixcmp entry in the Media Types registry now refers here instead of to RFC 2510.
  • The same media type in the CoAP Content-Formats registry now refers here instead of to RFC 4210.
  • The cmp entry in the Well-Known URIs registry now refers here instead of to RFC 4210.
  • The p entry in the CMP Well-Known URI Path Segments registry now refers here instead of to RFC 9480.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone book entries for CMP now list this document as the place to look.
